title: How KV Cache Prefetch Cuts Storage Latency
title_hi: केवी कैश प्रीफ़ेच स्टोरेज लेटेंसी को कैसे कम करता है
summary: Reduce storage latency with KV Cache prefetch
content: KV Cache data prefetch reduces storage latency in large-model inference. Measured on the Mingxin FX100, it improves inference throughput by 29-40% and reduces time-to-first-token by 26-32%. This is because KV Cache reads are taking up a large share of latency composition. As context windows expand, KV Cache capacity requirements grow, but GPU HBM capacity growth lags behind. Prefetch strips storage latency out of the inference critical path, so compute units no longer wait on data. The primary test platform was 8× AMD Instinct MI308X, running Qwen3-Coder-480B-FP8.
content_hi: केवी कैश डेटा प्रीफ़ेच बड़े-मॉडल इन्फरेंस में स्टोरेज लेटेंसी को कम करता है। मिंगजिन एफएक्स100 पर मापा गया, यह इन्फरेंस थ्रूपुट को 29-40% बढ़ाता है और समय-से-पहले-टोकन को 26-32% कम करता है। केवी कैश पढ़ने लेटेंसी संरचना में एक बड़ा हिस्सा ले रहे हैं। संदर्भ विंडोज़ के विस्तार के साथ, केवी कैश क्षमता आवश्यकताएं बढ़ती हैं, लेकिन जीपीयू एचबीएम क्षमता वृद्धि पीछे रह जाती है।

title: Optimizing Storage for AI Inference
title_hi: एआई अनुमान के लिए स्टोरेज का चयन
summary: AI storage optimization
content: When it comes to selecting storage for domestic AI computing centers, the key is to match KV Cache access patterns. Inference workloads exhibit high-concurrency, low-latency, and high-bandwidth random read/write patterns, differing from training scenarios. A storage solution optimized for KV Cache can improve inference throughput by 29-40%. The selection process involves balancing bandwidth, capacity, and cost. Bandwidth requirements are determined by the GPU cluster's aggregate memory access capability, with PCIe generation and network protocol defining the I/O ceiling.

title: Claude Code Now Runs Subagents in the Background by Default

content: Claude Code has undergone a significant change, now running subagents in the background by default. title: Why HTML Templates Are Still the Fastest, Cheapest Way to Launch a Small Business Website
title_hi: Why HTML Templates Are Still the Fastest, Cheapest Way to Launch a Small Business Website
summary:
Why HTML Templates Are Still the Fastest, Cheapest Way to Launch a Small Business Website


AI website builders
content:
Why HTML Templates Are Still the Fastest, Cheapest Way to Launch a Small Business Website


AI website builders are having a moment. Platforms like Wix ADI, Squarespace Blueprint, and a wave of newer AI-first tools promise to have your website live in minutes — just answer a few questions, and let the algorithm do the rest. It sounds like a dream for small business owners.

But here's what the marketing doesn't tell you: for many local and service-based businesses, a professionally designed HTML template still gets you online faster, for less money, and with more control. Let's break down why.





  
  
  The Real Cost of "Free" AI Website Builders


Most AI website builders operate on subscription models. The entry-level plans that actually let you connect a custom domain and remove branding badges typically run $12–$25/month — that's $144–$300 per year, every year, for as long as you need a website.

A quality HTML template, by contrast, is a one-time purchase. You pay once, download the files, and host them on any affordable static hosting service (or even free tiers from platforms like Netlify or GitHub Pages). Over three years, the cost difference can run into the hundreds of dollars.





  
  
  Speed: Templates Win When You Know What You Want


The pitch behind AI builders is speed. But "speed" depends on what you're comparing. If you've ever tried getting a generic AI site to match your exact brand colors, swap out a stock photo layout, or move a section to a different position — you know how that session can spiral into an afternoon of dragging, refreshing, and waiting for previews to load.

With an HTML template, you get clean, readable code. A developer (or a business owner comfortable with basic HTML) can make targeted changes in minutes. No proprietary drag-and-drop editor, no locked-in page builder, no loading spinners.

For trades and service businesses especially — HVAC companies, handymen, cleaning services — the page structure is almost always the same: a hero section, a services list, a trust-builder section, and a contact form. A well-made template has all of that ready to go. You're filling in your details, not designing from scratch.





  
  
  The Right Template for Your Industry Already Exists


One underrated advantage of the HTML template market is specialization. Rather than starting with a blank AI canvas and describing your business in a text prompt, you can browse templates built specifically for your niche — with layouts, color schemes, and content sections that already reflect how customers in your industry expect to navigate a website.

Looking to launch a site for an HVAC business? A purpose-built HVAC website template will already have sections for service areas, emergency call CTAs, and equipment highlights — none of which an AI builder will intuit on its own without significant prompting and tweaking.

The same logic applies to trades businesses. A handyman website template comes pre-structured for the things that convert handyman leads: a service list, a before/after gallery, and a prominent "Request a Quote" button. You're not teaching a builder what a handyman site should look like — it already knows.

And for residential and commercial cleaning businesses, a cleaning service website template gives you a polished, trust-focused layout that would take hours to replicate from scratch in any AI builder, however smart.





  
  
  You Own What You Build


This is the point most small business owners don't think about until it's too late: when you build on an AI website platform, you don't own the website — you own a subscription to it.

If the platform raises prices, shuts down, or changes its terms, your site is at risk. You can't export a Wix site and host it somewhere else. You can't take your Squarespace pages to a cheaper host when your business is watching costs.

With an HTML template, the files are yours. Host them anywhere. Move them anytime. Hand them off to a developer without platform lock-in. For a small business that's watching every dollar, that kind of flexibility has real long-term value.





  
  
  When AI Builders Do Make Sense


To be fair, AI website builders aren't the wrong choice for everyone. If you have no technical comfort whatsoever, need live e-commerce features out of the box, or want ongoing content management through a non-technical CMS, a subscription platform may be worth the cost.

But for the majority of local service businesses — the plumbers, cleaners, consultants, and contractors who need a clean, professional web presence with a phone number and a contact form — an HTML template delivers everything necessary at a fraction of the ongoing cost.





  
  
  The Bottom Line


AI website builders are impressive technology. But impressive technology isn't always the right tool for the job. For small businesses that want to launch fast, spend less, and keep control of their online presence, a well-designed HTML template remains one of the smartest moves available.

The best website for your business isn't the one built by the most advanced AI — it's the one that loads quickly, looks professional, and turns visitors into customers. HTML templates have been doing exactly that for years. They're not going anywhere.

title: Your Rails App Isn't Too Old for AI. It's Too Untested.
title_hi: Your Rails App Isn't Too Old for AI. It's Too Untested.

content:
When an AI feature fails to land on a legacy Rails app, it is almost never the model. It is that nobody could safely change the code underneath it.

We picked up an app running Rails 5.2 with 11% test coverage and a Sidekiq queue nobody had looked at since 2021. The team had already built an LLM classifier. It worked on a laptop and had been sitting in a branch for five months, because merging it meant touching a controller that three people were afraid of.

That is the whole argument: modernization is not a rewrite and it is not a version bump. It is the sequence that makes a legacy Rails app changeable again, and then puts AI in the places where the numbers move. Skip the sequence and you get a prototype that lives in a branch forever.


  
  
  The sequence, and why you don't get to reorder it


Audit, upgrade, test, refactor, then integrate. Every step exists because the next one is unsafe without it.



Audit. Map dependencies, security posture, and tech debt against business priorities. You are deciding what not to touch as much as what to fix.

Upgrade, one major at a time. 4.2 → 5.0 → 5.2 → 6.0 → 6.1 → 7.0 → 7.2 → 8.0. Resolve deprecations at each stop and enable new defaults gradually through config.load_defaults. Skipping a version to save a sprint buys you a month of breaking changes.

Test. Unit, integration, and system coverage, running on every push in CI. This is not hygiene. It is the precondition for everything after it.

Refactor. Extract business logic into service objects and concerns. This is where the seams for AI actually get cut.

Integrate. Only now.


Incremental work also wins on cost - rebuilds have been measured at up to three times the feature development cost of upgrading in place. And there are still over 560,000 live Rails sites, so the population of teams making this decision is not small.


  
  
  What the AI layer actually looks like


Four components, and none of them are optional if the feature is going to survive a production week.
A provider client. Wrap OpenAI, Anthropic, Hugging Face, or your self-hosted model behind one abstraction. Swap vendors without touching business logic. Swap in a mock during CI so tests are fast and deterministic.
A service object. All AI logic lives here. Testable, replaceable, out of the controller.
A background job. Sidekiq or equivalent. Model calls never sit in the request path. A recommendation engine can chew through user data without adding a millisecond to page load.
**An audit table. **Inputs, outputs, and confidence scores in JSONB on Postgres. When a classification is wrong, you pull the exact pair, fix the prompt, and version the change.

The trade-off nobody puts in the proposal: that audit table grows fast and someone has to own retention on it.


  
  
  How do you keep the AI layer from quietly costing you money?


Set confidence thresholds before launch, not after the first invoice. When confidence drops below the line, fall back to deterministic logic, a cached prior answer, or a human review queue. Enforce a per-tenant daily cost cap at the job layer, where you can actually stop the work.
Then treat prompts as versioned, testable code and mock model responses in the suite. An untested prompt change is a production change with no rollback story.


  
  
  When to bring someone in


In-house works when the team ships weekly, has bandwidth for a 20% side program, and the AI use case is scoped tightly. Bring in help when:


Rails is two or more majors behind and no engineer on the team has run an upgrade this decade.
A live prototype never got past staging because nobody owns operations for it.
A board or regulator has set a date, and missing it has a number attached.
The one senior Rails engineer who understood the plan just gave notice.


What to push back on in a vendor quote: any multi-month discovery phase that ends in a slide deck, any proposal naming juniors on delivery, any pricing without a locked scope.
None of this shows up in a demo. It shows up five months later, when the classifier still works perfectly on someone's laptop and the branch has 400 commits of drift behind main. The upgrade sequence is not the interesting part of adding AI to Rails. It is the part that decides whether the AI ever ships.
